news.title: Goldman Sachs revealed its outlook for 2027. Here’s how much it sees the S&P 500 gaining
news.summary:
Goldman Sachs’ 2027 S&P 500 outlook:
- Expected 2027 return: about 17% gain to around 8,700 by year-end.
- 2027 earnings growth: projected to slow to about 18% (down from ~30% in 2026), as AI-related capital spending decelerates.
- 2028: continuation of slower earnings growth and a moderating equity return profile.
- Key risks: if earnings estimates drop to the 30-year trend and P/E compress to the 30-year average (17x), the S&P 500 could fall to around 5,600 (~23% downside). Conversely, stronger-than-expected earnings or AI capex could lift the index toward ~9,400 (nearly +30%).
- Market theme: AI benefits broadening beyond builders/enablers to adopters and users; hyperscalers and buyback leaders may outperform.
- Sector/investment views: energy infrastructure could show acceleration; health care and consumer staples offer stability and diversification.

Bottom line: Goldman sees a continued bull market into 2027 but with more modest gains and rising risk from earnings trajectory and AI-related spending, with substantial upside if earnings resilience or AI productivity surprises emerge.

Be selective and maintain diversification; avoid over-allocating to semis or overcrowded AI trades. Use volatility to add selectively to U.S. stocks rather than chasing the hot AI names.

Bottom line: The committee argues the bull market remains intact with a healthier, more investable backdrop for Nasdaq tech stocks, provided investors stay selective, focused on quality, and maintain diversification.

news.title: Strategists say investors should start asking 'what could go right' after tech's 42% valuation reset | Morningstar
news.summary:
Investors should shift from pessimism to potential upside in tech after a sharp valuation reset. Key points:

- Tech valuations have fallen ~42% over the past year, one of the steepest drops in ~30 years, with the Nasdaq down ~12% since its Oct high. 
- Strategists Keith Lerner and Jake Reid of Truist Advisory Services say the reset sets up a potential rebound if earnings cuts prove milder than feared or minimal, suggesting the downside is already priced in.
- The backdrop is different from past crises: valuations are now below levels at the start of the current bull market in late 2022, and the AI buildout remains underway.
- They caution returns won’t be linear, given debt concerns and monetization uncertainties, but note historical tech drawdowns have often followed with meaningful rebounds (average ~47% after 6 declines >10% in a bull run).
- Truist recommends investors who’ve reduced exposure (e.g., to XLK) to view current weakness as a buying opportunity, anticipating that prices may rally before headlines improve.

Bottom line for a Nasdaq tech stock outlook: after a sharp valuation reset, downside risk appears largely priced in, and a favorable setup may emerge if earnings cuts are less severe than feared and AI investment persists; expect non-linear moves with potential for a notable rebound.

news.title: Why Central Bank Buying Is Keeping Gold Afloat as More Fed Hikes Are Expected
news.summary:
Summary:
- Gold faces pressure from higher expected Fed rate hikes and a stronger U.S. dollar, which reduce gold’s relative appeal since the metal doesn’t pay interest.
- Real yields on 10-year Treasuries remain elevated (2.84% today) and the dollar index is near 19-month highs, both bearish for gold’s price.
- Near-term resilience is supported by central banks buying aggressively: the World Gold Council reports 321 metric tons purchased in Q3 (up 42% YoY) and 675 tons for the year, suggesting price support as buyers diversify from the dollar.
- Investor flow is mixed: U.S. investors pulled $1.8B from the largest gold fund in October, while global funds accumulated about $2.7B, with Europe and Asia driving demand.
- Historical context from the WGC study indicates gold tends to recover when: gold is well below long-term trend, the dollar spikes, and futures positioning has compressed. Today two of these three conditions are present (big gap below trend and strong dollar); speculative positioning remains near its 20-year average.
- Outlook note: While a bottom is not guaranteed and timing is uncertain, one more shakeout before a durable floor is possible, with potential for a rebound if a false breakdown is validated and technical support holds.

Key macro drivers to watch:
- Fed path: expectations of multiple 25bp rate hikes through next year heighten real yield and dollar strength, weighing on gold.
- Inflation split: services inflation and energy costs persist, complicating the inflation outlook and policy stance.
- Central bank demand: ongoing purchases provide price support and can cushion downturns, even amid rising yields.
- Speculative positioning: large traders remain net long; a shift could precede another leg lower or a stabilization, depending on price action and macro data.

Bottom line: The outlook is highly sensitive to Fed policy signals; ongoing rate hikes and potential ETF selling pressure imply a risk of further near-term weakness even as longer-run fundamentals remain constructive if central banks continue buying and inflation cools.

news.title: Global crude surplus will reach 2 million b/d in 2027: Goldman Sachs | S&P Global
news.summary:
Goldman Sachs expects a global crude supply surplus of about 2 million barrels per day in 2027. Key drivers:
- Persian Gulf output set to rise by ~4 million b/d vs. current levels.
- Pipeline bypass capacity to reach ~3.8 million b/d next year, routing Gulf barrels around the Strait of Hormuz via new UAE West-East pipeline, Saudi repurposed gas pipeline, and Yanbu expansion.
- By end-2027, Gulf exports able to bypass Hormuz to about 14 million b/d (~60% of 2025 average exports).
- Gulf liquids output to rise ~4 million b/d from Oct 2026 to 2027, lifting global stock balances to a 2 million b/d surplus (production minus end-use demand).
- Global oil demand projected to recover to prewar trend outside China; China’s demand peak in 2025 and slower growth going forward.
Price outlook:
- Brent expected to average ~$88/b in 2027, easing to ~$78/b by year-end 2027.
- Near-term risk premium to unwind as Middle East refining capacity returns.
- Dated Brent around $96/b (Nov 13) but other forecasts (CERA) show higher near-term prices then decline through 2027–2028.
Other notes:
- US diesel prices expected around $150/b next year; US margins could remain tight in 2027.
- Global refining capacity growth modest (400k b/d in 2027; 300k b/d in 2028), potentially unable to offset Russian product declines if demand recovers.
- Persian Gulf product exports likely remain well below 2025 averages due to refinery damage, transport risks, and transfer challenges.
- Ongoing Middle East conflict and maintenance support for product prices if tanker disruptions persist.

news.title: Goldman Sachs sees supply surplus as Fed faces inflation risks
news.summary:
Summary:
- Goldman Sachs argues that falling crude oil prices do not guarantee lower inflation because refined-product bottlenecks (damaged refineries, limited capacity, higher transport costs) can keep gasoline, diesel, and other products costly.
- Even with higher crude oil supplies, refined-product prices may stay above historical averages into 2027, meaning energy inflation could persist even as crude prices drop.
- This decoupling occurs because refining limits and transport costs can cushion carries to consumers, with diesel being particularly influential due to its use in transport, industry, and agriculture.
- The Fed faces a dilemma: high energy and service costs can linger despite lower crude prices, and tighter monetary policy can dampen demand but not fix physical energy supply constraints immediately.
- The macro outlook hinges on whether improvements in crude oil conditions translate into meaningful, sustained energy-price relief for households and businesses, and how Treasury yields, credit spreads, and financing conditions evolve.
- The critical question for 2027 is less about the oil price level and more about whether energy-supply improvements reduce inflationary pressures in time to support a stable monetary policy, without triggering higher defaults or financial stress.

news.title: Oil Market Weekly: The Glut Is Back, but the Tank Is Still Running on Empty | Investing.com
news.summary:
The article argues that while the crude market’s *flow* is improving (global supply is moving from a deficit toward a surplus), the *physical* oil system is still constrained—especially in refined products—so crude price weakness may not quickly translate into cheaper energy for consumers.

Key points:
- **Inventory trend has flipped, but the “hangover” remains:** Inventories began building again in October (average **+1.7 million bpd**), after months of drawdowns. JPMorgan sees the depletion phase ending, but Morgan Stanley’s tracking suggests a large weekly inflow into inventories in November.  
- **Crude is recovering faster than refined fuels:** Even with more crude available, **refined-product stocks (diesel/jet fuel)** remain relatively depressed. The author attributes this to **refinery/export constraints** (Middle East shipping risks around **Hormuz**, and **Ukrainian attacks** affecting Russian processing).  
- **Why Brent can fall while diesel/jet stay expensive:** The macro implication is that falling crude prices may take longer to ease inflation because the bottleneck is in **refining and finished-product availability**, not just crude supply.  
- **Base-case for lower prices is conditional:** A **$50–$70 Brent** range is discussed as plausible if Gulf shipments normalize, refinery bottlenecks ease, and a future surplus materializes—but the author warns not to rely on it yet because disruptions could quickly reintroduce a geopolitical premium.  
- **What to watch next week:** Continued **inventory builds**, whether **refined-product stocks catch up to crude**, and whether the **options market range narrows** while security risks persist.

Overall, the author’s macro stance is **directionally bearish for Brent**, but with the caveat that the refined-product “repair” is incomplete, which can limit how fast crude-driven relief reaches real-world prices.

news.title: World Bank: global agricultural prices set to rise by 5.3 per cent in 2027 - Il Sole 24 ORE
news.summary:
World Bank’s October Commodity Markets Outlook projects a 5.3% rise in the overall agricultural commodities price index in 2027, driven by ongoing supply challenges and climate-related risks, with energy costs and biofuel raw material demand adding to upward pressure. Key points:
- 2026-27 outlook: Brent crude expected to ease from $91/bbl (2026) to ~$79/bbl, helping energy markets but not fully offsetting agricultural price gains.
- 2027 forecast: Agricultural and food commodities up 5.3% overall; food products inflation projected at ~7.2% in 2027.
- Hotspots: Cereals, vegetable oils, and protein flours face upward pressure. US hard red winter wheat could rise ~28% in Dec 2026, then +13.5% in 2027. Rice (Thailand benchmark) +11.6% in 2027 after weather-related 2026 declines.
- Soya oil: +11.4% in 2027 (after +39% in 2026), driven by biorefinery demand and production issues. Palm oil supported by El Niño-related supply risks.
- Cocoa: 2026 decline expected (-37.2%) due to Ivory Coast/Ghana recovery; 2027 rebound ~+10.2% amid West Africa uncertainties.
- Coffee: Expect gradual price normalisation with declines for Arabica and Robusta as production recovers.
- Fertilisers: Near-term spike in 2026 followed by a correction in 2027; nitrogen and phosphate (UREA down ~15.9%, DAP down ~18%) weighed by energy market normalisation.
- Underlying drivers: Geopolitical tensions, export/logistics constraints (Black Sea), El Niño effects on harvests, rising production costs, and biofuel demand.

Overall takeaway for agricultural commodities market outlook: a renewed price upcycle in 2027 amidst persistent supply and climate-driven risks, with some relief in energy and fertiliser markets helping moderate gains.

news.title: FX Daily: Don’t mess with the dollar near term | ING THINK
news.summary: Summary: ING FX Daily on 13 November argues the US dollar remains firmly bid near term due to hot US inflation data and hawkish Fed expectations. A stronger path for Fed tightening (potential December 50bp, perhaps followed by January) supports higher yields and a stronger dollar. DXY could push to around 104.60 next, with EUR/USD under pressure toward 1.08 and USD/JPY rallying through 160. Key risk factors include the October PPI data, components feeding the Fed’s PCE target (healthcare, airfares, software), and potential shifts if core PCE cools unexpectedly. The euro area is seen as struggling to out-hawk the Fed, keeping EUR/USD vulnerable, with a possible year-end break below 1.10. Overall, the dollar’s strength is likely to persist into the coming weeks unless USD-driven catalysts (e.g., a sharp tech sell-off or unexpected ECB hawkishness) emerge.

Summary:
- The US dollar (DXY) is breaking higher as US financial conditions tighten at an unusually fast pace. Historical patterns around rapid tightening suggest the dollar often strengthens in these episodes, supporting a bullish bias for now.
- Technical setup remains bullish: a breakout from a falling wedge, with the price reclaiming 102.945 and testing above 103.35. Next upside target eyed at 104.68 (March 2025 high), then 105.44 as a minor level.
- Momentum indicators are positive (MACD rising, RSI above 50) but RSI has not yet made a new high in price, so no bearish divergence yet.
- On the downside, a drop below 103.35 could shift focus to 102.945, then 102.49, with a broader support zone near 101 (including 38.2% Fibonacci retracement at 101.138).
- Key risk to the bullish view: a shift to dovish Fed policy or weaker US data that dampens rate expectations; otherwise, the macro backdrop and recent surprises keep the bullish DXY outlook intact.
